items.summary: Saudi Arabia has launched a series of strikes on a strategic oil depot on the outskirts of Yemen’s capital, Sana’a, while later on Tuesday it said it had intercepted missiles launched toward Dharan, location of the headquarters of the huge national energy company Saudi Aramco. The attacks on both sides were a fresh escalation of the conflict between Riyadh and the Iran-backed Houthi forces. Before its offensive on Tuesday, a Saudi spokesperson warned civilians to leave the target area, in an apparent attempt to strike fear into the local population before the biggest attack so far on Houthi energy infrastructure. The Central Sabaha Station oil depot on the western side of the city contains large tanks that often hold substantial quantities of fuel derivatives, although the Yemeni Oil Company said its storage facilities were empty at the time of the attack. Houthi oil depots at the Ras Isa port in Hodeidah, the subject of Israeli attacks in 2024, were also struck in 10 waves of attacks apparently aimed at immobilising the Houthi army as it continues its push south, including towards the city of Taiz. Earlier the Saudis also struck what they believe to be a Houthi leadership hide-out in the Bani Mu’in area in the Razih border district, west of Saada governorate, northern Yemen. The strike on the oil depot appeared to be the Saudi response to a Houthi attack on King Khalid international airport in Riyadh on Saturday that killed 13 people and left 300 injured.

items.originalTitle: US Army targets 2028 for first high-energy laser counter-drone weapons
items.summary: The first directed energy weapon selected by the U.S. Army for the Enduring-High Energy Laser (E-HEL) program could be out of testing and ready for counter-drone operations by early 2028, Army officials told Military Times at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting in Washington. “We would love to be able to keep the first unit off the line for our testing and training. However, what we’ve seen is, with the environment as it is, everything that we produce as a capable counter-UAS system tends to get deployed somewhere,” said Kirk Williams, chief engineer at the U.S. Army Directed Energy Project Office. In September, the Army awarded AeroVironment a $464.8 million contract for LOCUST X3, its modular, palletized high-energy laser system. Earlier generations of the LOCUST system are actively fielded in operational environments, including at the U.S. southern border, according to AeroVironment. The first LOCUST X3 is slated for delivery by Q4 of FY 2027 and will be mounted on the Joint Light Tactical Vehicle. The goal is to push it through testing, validation, verification and “give it to soldiers as soon as possible,” said Brig. Gen. Guy Yelverton, capability program executive for Defensive Fires. “My far-down point would be spring [2028], and if I could get in the December-January timeframe, that would be awesome. That would be a great win for the Army.” It is unclear where the first high-energy counter-drone weapons under H-ELS will be deployed. Yelverton suggested the 7th Infantry Division could be a potential partner.

items.title: US Army assesses Trust Automation’s integrated drone defence system
items.originalTitle: US Army assesses Trust Automation’s integrated drone defence system
items.summary: Trust Automation has completed a US Army operational assessment of its Small-Unmanned Air Defense System (SUADS) during a National Training Center rotation at Fort Irwin, California. Conducted with the 703rd Brigade Support Battalion, 2nd Armored Brigade Combat Team, 3rd Infantry Division, the assessment evaluated SUADS in a large-scale combat operations training environment under ongoing uncrewed aerial system (UAS) threats. During the rotation, Trust Automation’s SUADS detected and engaged UAS between approximately two and six kilometres away, with potential coverage extending to approximately seven kilometres under favourable conditions, the company said in a 12 October press release. Interview participants were not aware of any enemy UAS that penetrated the defended area as a threat within the identified operational ranges without first being detected by the system. Trust Automation’s integrated system combined radar, electro-optical/infrared (EO/IR) sensors, NINJA and DroneBuster technologies. MAJ Patrick Smith, Battalion Executive Officer said the system consistently provided layered surveillance, early warning, positive target identification and electronic defeat of hostile UAS before enemy systems could successfully conduct reconnaissance, target acquisition or attack missions. SUADS brings multiple sensors and effectors into a single integrated system while enabling individual technologies to be added or upgraded as capabilities and threats evolve. Trust Automation is also developing a mobile SUADS variant to support tactical units where forces move frequently.

history.title: PAC-3 Edge Will Be The Most Capable Patriot Interceptor Ever
history.originalTitle: PAC-3 Edge Will Be The Most Capable Patriot Interceptor Ever

evidenceRecords.text: Lockheed Martin has unveiled the PAC-3 Edge, a new interceptor that would represent the top tier of the U.S. Army’s Patriot air defense missile family.

The missile is being developed to deliver greater performance against advanced threats than the current PAC-3 Missile Segment Enhancement (MSE), as the Army advances a competition for its next-generation interceptor.
The PAC-3 Edge displayed at the Association of the U.S. Army’s (AUSA) main annual convention.
Howard Altman The company says PAC-3 Edge will offer improved performance against increasingly challenging aerial threats, including advanced ballistic and hypersonic missiles.
The design builds on the PAC-3 MSE’s existing technology while incorporating a new seeker, an upgraded control system, and a more advanced solid rocket motor developed with Northrop Grumman.
In terms of appearance, PAC-3 Edge differs significantly from the PAC-3 MSE.
An overview of the improvements found on the PAC-3 MSE variant over its predecessors.
The Army previously abandoned its Lower-Tier Future Interceptor (LTFI) program in 2024, citing cost concerns, and instead emphasized incremental improvements to the existing PAC-3 MSE.
A PAC-3 interceptor seen at the moment of launch.

U.S. Department of Defense A More Capable Patriot Interceptor PAC-3 Edge is intended to preserve the advantages of the existing PAC-3 family while improving the missile’s ability to engage targets at longer ranges and higher altitudes.

Tim Cahill, president of Missiles and Fire Control (MFC) for Lockheed Martin, told TWZ that the same seeker technology that will be used in PAC-3 Edge will also find its way into future offensive and defensive systems going into the future.

To ensure greater agility, Jason Reynolds, vice president and general manager of Integrated Air and Missile Defense (IAMD) at Lockheed Martin, explained that the new missile adds a greater number of more capable attitude control motors (ACMs), compared to the PAC-3 MSE.

Lockheed Martin is weighing new industry partnerships to produce urgently needed PAC-3 Patriot interceptors in Europe, an avenue that could also help fill Ukraine’s shortfalls, a company executive said.

Discussions about producing more Patriot interceptors outside the United States have picked up steam since Ukrainian leaders said over the summer they were promised by the Trump administration a license to make them in Ukraine to defend against Russian missile and drone barrages.
U.S. government officials are still expected to make a decision, which could entail the production of PAC-2 interceptors, made by Raytheon, or Lockheed’s PAC-3.

“From a PAC-3 perspective, we’re absolutely willing to talk to Ukraine,” Jason Reynolds, vice president and general manager of the company’s integrated air and missile defense division, told Defense News in an interview at the Association of the United States Army annual convention in Washington, DC.

Patriot interceptor deliveries to Poland will be delayed, top general says “It’s really a matter of what’s their industrial capability, what’s the parts availability, those types of things,” he continued.

“It might be something like an ACE, as opposed to an MSE, that we would start with for Ukraine.” Lockheed announced development of an ACE variant during the summer, billing it as a cheaper option against relatively simple threats — at half the cost of an MSE missile designed to go against sophisticated missiles.

The new interceptor will make do with a single-pulse motor, compared with a dual-pulse of the MSE interceptor, and utilize a blast fragmentation warhead, versus the direct hit-to-kill mechanics of the MSE missile.
Reynolds cautioned that setting up interceptor missile production of whatever variant in Ukraine comes with the risk of Russian attacks on the plant.

“If we can get that started, get the supply chain started and then migrate to Ukraine as an option, that would make a lot of sense to me.” Germany is among the countries where leaders have offered to host PAC-3 production .

For an eventual PAC-3 production, Lockheed is considering partnering with Diehl Defence, with which there is a cooperation agreement on interceptor parts in place dating from October 2025, Reynolds said.

evidenceRecords.text: Echodyne and Allen Control Systems (ACS) have signed a collaboration agreement to develop, demonstrate and deploy integrated counter-uncrewed aerial system (C-UAS) technologies and platforms.
The companies said that the new agreement reflects a joint commitment to open architectures, rapid integration and commercial manufacturing for systems that can be fielded at scale.

The agreement establishes collaboration across Echodyne’s C-UAS radar hardware and software systems and ACS’s Bullfrog robotic weapon station capabilities, and follows the recent announcement of each company’s award from the United States’ Joint Interagency Task Force 401 (JIATF-401) for Domestic Shield, the JIATF-401 C-UAS Marketplace and other C-UAS requirements.

“Bullfrog combines computer vision, autonomous control and precision robotics with existing weapon systems to detect, track, identify and engage unmanned threats,” Echodyne said in a 12 October press release.
The company’s radar track data will extend this capability with persistent airspace positional information.

EchoShield generates location and velocity data for a wide range of drone types and flight profiles, and the system’s open interfaces enables radar data to flow directly into Bullfrog and broader command-and-control (C2) platforms.
Echodyne’s MESA radar architecture delivers electronically scanned array capabilities.
Maritime operations are one focus of the collaboration, with EchoShield increasingly integrated aboard uncrewed surface vessels for maritime awareness and C-UAS missions.
Echodyne and ACS will continue integrated testing and participation in US defence department demonstration events designed to evaluate the combined system under representative operational conditions.
The companies expect these activities to inform further product integration and support customer requirements across fixed-site, mobile, expeditionary and maritime missions.

topicPlan.title: 拦截弹产能为何成了美欧防务最紧的瓶颈
topicPlan.angle: 本篇回答一个具体问题：美国拦截弹的产能扩张究竟卡在哪个环节，为什么在乌克兰与中东需求下仍难以放量。现在值得写，是因为同一天有两条互相印证的进展：洛克希德评估在欧洲、乌克兰本地生产PAC-3，而此前一周该公司刚公布PAC-3 Edge并在更早与五角大楼签下七年框架协议、把年产能目标从约600枚提到约2000枚，Boeing也锁定了导引头产能翻三倍的七年协议。这些报道属于同一项目与同一条产能追踪议题，能拼出从整弹到关键部件、从美国本土到欧洲与乌克兰的完整链条。靠这些证据可以讲清机制——瓶颈不只在总装，更在导引头、固体发动机等上游环节和许可、工业基础条件；也可以讲清约束与尚不知道的事：欧洲或乌克兰生产是否获批、PAC-3与雷神PAC-2哪条线被选中、2000枚年产能何时真正兑现。

topicPlan.title: 反无人机竞赛：2028年激光上阵前谁先补上库存空缺
topicPlan.angle: 本篇回答反无人机能力建设的路径之争：在定向能武器真正成军之前，美欧靠什么补上拦截弹与传感器缺口。现在值得写，是因为同一天出现了三条方向不同但同属反无人机追踪议题的报道——美陆军把首型高能激光反无人机武器的测试完成与部署目标定在2028年初并已授予LOCUST X3合同，康斯伯格宣布在波兰投建反无人机系统新厂配套San系统，通用动力在AUSA展出PERCH 2.0、M-SHORAD增量4与Leonidas等反无人机方案。三者分别代表激光、欧洲本地化弹药与探测、平台层集成三条路线，合起来能说明为什么短期内仍要靠导弹和电子手段过渡、激光何时可能改变成本结构。可以横向比较各家路线的成熟度差异，并指出尚不知道的关键点：LOCUST X3按计划2027财年四季度首台交付但2028年才具备作战能力，波兰工厂的出口与产能爬坡节奏，以及这些系统是否与开放接口的C2体系真正互通。

evidenceRecords.text: EOS Defense Systems USA has unveiled plans for a next-generation version of its Slinger counter-uncrewed aircraft system (C-UAS) remote weapon system, with US production scheduled to begin at the company’s Huntsville, Alabama facility in 2027.

EOS said selectable autonomy will allow the system to respond to drone threats at a faster decision cycle, while retaining the current Slinger’s stabilised capability to engage targets while on the move.

history.title: Echodyne and Allen Control Systems ink C-UAS collaboration deal
history.originalTitle: Echodyne and Allen Control Systems ink C-UAS collaboration deal

evidenceRecords.text: Echodyne and Allen Control Systems (ACS) have signed a collaboration agreement to develop, demonstrate and deploy integrated counter-uncrewed aerial system (C-UAS) technologies and platforms.
The companies said that the new agreement reflects a joint commitment to open architectures, rapid integration and commercial manufacturing for systems that can be fielded at scale.

The agreement establishes collaboration across Echodyne’s C-UAS radar hardware and software systems and ACS’s Bullfrog robotic weapon station capabilities, and follows the recent announcement of each company’s award from the United States’ Joint Interagency Task Force 401 (JIATF-401) for Domestic Shield, the JIATF-401 C-UAS Marketplace and other C-UAS requirements.

“Bullfrog combines computer vision, autonomous control and precision robotics with existing weapon systems to detect, track, identify and engage unmanned threats,” Echodyne said in a 12 October press release.
The company’s radar track data will extend this capability with persistent airspace positional information.

EchoShield generates location and velocity data for a wide range of drone types and flight profiles, and the system’s open interfaces enables radar data to flow directly into Bullfrog and broader command-and-control (C2) platforms.
Echodyne’s MESA radar architecture delivers electronically scanned array capabilities.
Maritime operations are one focus of the collaboration, with EchoShield increasingly integrated aboard uncrewed surface vessels for maritime awareness and C-UAS missions.
Echodyne and ACS will continue integrated testing and participation in US defence department demonstration events designed to evaluate the combined system under representative operational conditions.
The companies expect these activities to inform further product integration and support customer requirements across fixed-site, mobile, expeditionary and maritime missions.

evidenceRecords.text: WARSAW, Poland — Norway’s Kongsberg has decided to build a new production facility for counter-drone systems in northern Poland, with plans to invest more than 200 million zloty ($51 million) in the plant.
The investment is connected to the company’s cooperation with Polish state-run defense group PGZ to deliver the San anti-drone system to the Polish military.
“We have been present in Poland for many years.

We think it’s important that we establish local sites in Poland,” Eirik Lie, the president and CEO of Kongsberg, told Defense News at the Warsaw Security Forum here on Oct. 12. “We are on good track for deliveries on the San program.
But also, we expect export contracts, so this enables us to be prepared for these exports from Poland.”

Under the San deal, valued at around PLN 15 billion ($3.8 billion), Kongsberg and PGZ are to supply 18 anti-drone batteries, 52 firing platoons, 18 command platoons, and 703 vehicles to the Polish military, according to data from Poland’s Ministry of National Defence.
The contract will be largely financed by loans that Poland has secured from the European Union’s Security Action For Europe (SAFE) scheme.
In a statement, the Norwegian group said it plans to sign a construction contract by the end of 2026 and begin work immediately afterward.
Serial production of counter-drone systems could begin in the first half of 2028.
The investment is expected to create more than 100 jobs in Poland once the plant reaches full capacity.

The Army initially experimented with Switchblade 600 before asking the company to focus on the smaller Switchblade 300, according to Taylor.

General Dynamics Land Systems continued developing PERCH 2.0 with its own independent research and development funding before the Army contracted for three additional prototypes under the Abrams program office.
The Army will evaluate the design after the experimentation and could compete the capability or purchase it, depending on the results, Taylor explained.
